## Nonholonomic systems
There are times when the Euler-Lagrange formulation with multipliers is the only way to include the constraints.

The **holonomic constraints** are functions of the generalized coordinates, and only of them:

$$
f(q_1, q_2,\dots,q_n)=0,
$$
and this is what we are used to apply, simple to differentiate

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial q_1} f \mathrm{d}q_1 + \frac{\partial}{\partial q_2} f \mathrm{d}q_2 + \dots + \frac{\partial}{\partial q_n} f \mathrm{d}q_n= 0.
$$

But there are cases where the constraint can only be expressed as a function of differentials $\mathrm{d}q_n$,

$$
A_1(q_1,\dots,q_n) \mathrm{d}q_1 + \dots + A_n(q_1,\dots,q_n) \mathrm{d}q_n= 0\,.
$$
These relations are, in general, **nonholonomic** constraints.

An example of these type of constraints is one that includes velocities, which in general can be written as

$$
f(q_i, \dot{q}_i, t)= 0,
$$
including the differentials $\frac{\mathrm{d}q_n}{\mathrm{d} t}$.

In just a few cases we can recover a $f(q_i,t)=0$ after integration (except when there are only two degrees of freedom, in which case it is always possible to integrate it), and check that it's actually a holonomic constraint.
An example of this is

$$
\sum_i A_i \dot{x}_i + B = 0\,.
$$

If $A_i = \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i} f$ and $B = \frac{\partial}{\partial t} f$ with $f=f(x_i, t)$, it can be rewritten as

$$
\sum_i \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i} f \frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} x_i + \frac{\partial}{\partial t} f = 0,
$$
since this is the total derivative with respect to time $\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d} t} f$, that can be integrated to get
$$
f(x_i,t) - \text{constant} = 0,
$$
showing that it is holonomic.

But if the constraint is written in differential form instead of an algebraic relation, we can incorporate it in the formulation with Lagrange multipliers, without the need of previous integrations, if this relation can be expressed as
$$
\sum_k \frac{\partial}{\partial q_i} f_k \mathrm{d}q_i = 0\,.
$$
The derivatives go in the last term along with the corresponding $\lambda_k(t)$.
This works even if there is an explicit function of time $\frac{\partial}{\partial t} f_k \mathrm{d} t$ in the constraint.
